text: A default matplotlib chart is a fine first draft for yourself. To show it to someone else, you customize it: line styles, reference lines, annotations, number formats, gridlines, and a consistent style. This lesson puts Lesson 3's layout habits into code.

Every plotting method takes keyword arguments for appearance: color, linewidth, linestyle, marker, and label. Draw the revenue line in a colorblind-safe blue, then add axhline for a dashed grey target line at 120. Anything with a label can show up in the legend.

Annotate points an arrow from a text position to a data point, perfect for labeling the one thing you want the reader to notice, here the September dip. set_title with loc equals left aligns the title with the axis and states the finding: revenue passed target in July, climbing from 115 in June to 124.3.

Format the y-axis with set_major_formatter so 140 becomes dollar 140 k. Draw faint horizontal gridlines only with grid axis equals y. Drop the legend's box with frameon equals False. And hide the top and right spines, the plot's own borders, to remove clutter.
The result: a bold line, a dashed grey target, a title that states the takeaway, and an arrow explaining the dip. Every element earns its place, nothing is there just to look busy.

Setting the same options on every chart is tedious, so set them once. plt dot style dot use applies a style sheet to every chart made afterward. plt dot rcParams is the dictionary of every default: fonts, line widths, colors, figure size. Put your preferred settings at the top of a notebook or in a shared module.

The test for every element you add: does it help the reader answer the question? A target line and a formatted axis do. A gradient background and a rainbow palette do not. Next lesson: seaborn, a library built on matplotlib for statistical plots.
